title: Think Hard, Work Hard, Remember More
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles proposes a single decision filter for school spending and curriculum choices, whether an option will help students work hard, think hard and remember more. He opens with the cautionary story of Sam Bankman-Fried, whose probabilistic thinking under imperfect information he borrows without the illegality. Five worked examples then apply the filter, covering outdoor seating versus exercise equipment, teaching assistants versus one SEND teacher, frequent exam practice versus two mocks, teacher-written model essays versus revision guides, and making rather than writing in DT. Several conclusions run against common school habits, which he playfully calls illegal. The method grounds resourcing decisions in retrieval, spacing and effort research rather than fashion.
points: A single question, whether a choice makes students work hard, think hard and remember more, makes resourcing decisions simpler and more consequential.
Short, frequent exam practice every few weeks beats two early full mocks, on the research on testing, retrieval, spacing and feedback.
Teacher-written model essays force student effort and also train teachers in structuring essays, which a bought revision guide does not.
Booklets and guides depend on student effort, which tends to be inconsistent, so they usually deliver less than designed lessons.
quotes: We have a lot more information in schools. It is easy to access. There’s research.
For me, this makes decision making easy, and forces those decisions to make more of a difference. (Example 1 is not academic - and examples 2-5 are).

It’s not even close. The research on testing, retrieval practice, spaced learning, the impact of feedback and our actual experience of mock results in November or December all suggest b) is a clear winner.
Option a) will make it very difficult for students not to work hard or think hard. They will remember a lot more of what will be tested, and how to organise their knowledge in an essay.

Option c) looks like the best of both worlds. But, it is a revision booklet, and therefore depends on the efforts of the students, which will be both inconsistent and probably too little. As a cohort, hey won’t work as hard, think as hard or remember as much.
Option b) will lead to many more students being better at making, both with a greater range of products and a higher degree of skill. So they will remember more of what they learn to do.
